column2: Two years after the summer of 1948, newly named head of the art department at Yale, Albers hires de Kooning as the first artist recruited to teach there. Consequences: A paradoxical reconciliation after the teaching affront

Theater-in-the-round version of Richards's Cocteau; a photograph by Hazel Larsen Archer shows June Rice Christensen as the photographer. June Rice Christensen as the photographer on stage; photograph by Archer

Josef is named chairman of the Department of Design at Yale; the Alberses settle in the New Haven area, where they live together until Josef's death and where Anni has stayed ever since. Consequences: A new life as a “faculty wife,” played down by Anni

When Josef paints his first Homage in 1950, Anni complains that they will never have enough to eat, that he has started painting Easter eggs. She soon becomes a discerning connoisseur of these works. Easter eggs
In 1950 Anni is delighted to receive $150 for a pictorial weaving; in the early 1960s she receives major architectural commissions and exhibits more often. $150
Before 1950 she mainly creates industrial designs; afterward she devotes herself almost exclusively to pictorial weavings.
Moves to New Haven, Connecticut

During the 1950s, Rice is one of fifteen authors invited to review great American books for a Carnegie Corporation project for libraries overseas, with the volume American Panorama. He reviews James Baldwin's Go Tell It on the Mountain. 15 authors

Motherwell asks de Kooning how he knows a painting is finished; de Kooning answers that he refrains from “finishing” it, that he paints himself out of the picture, then keeps it if it has a figure and throws it out if not.

Robert Motherwell reads his essay “The Renaissance and Order” at Studio 35 (published in 1951 in trans/formation); first show abroad, at the 25th Venice Biennale, selected by Alfred H. Barr; begins the third Women series; at Josef Albers's invitation, teaches at the Yale School of Fine Arts. Consequences: Albers renews his invitation, this time outside BMC

At some point in the 1950s, de Kooning traveled to Cuba; his fruitless search for Hemingway's house inspired the title Suburb in Havana (1958). Consequences: The painting's resolute amplitude refers as much to Hemingway's writing as to the place
Lecture published in trans/formation 1, 1951.

Josef takes up his teaching post at Yale; he and Anni choose a small Cape Cod house identical to their neighbors', unpretentious, made for living and working. Consequences: Twenty years later, better off thanks to the art boom, they buy the house on Birchwood Drive in Orange

The painting of a still life, followed by the author: Hofmann sets out a white bowl, three apples, an ashtray, a small jug, and a jar of poster paint against a backdrop of embossed silver paper, with a cellophane cone in the vase. After three hours he is holding fifteen brushes in his left hand; the paper backdrop collapses and shifts the objects, forcing him to follow only the logic of the picture; an eight-hour session the next day brings it to completion, and he goes back to it three times after beginning Fruit Bowl, No. II. Only four colors (white, red, blue, yellow), then crimson at the end; Permalba white; three hours of work, then eight hours the next day; fifteen brushes in the left hand; the still life will serve for six paintings in all; for the later ones the apples go into the bowl, a lemon is added, and the jug, the ashtray, and the paper cylinder are removed. Consequences: The Fruit Bowl series: Transubstantiation, No. I, II, III, etc.

A tube of pigment in one hand and a palette knife in the other, Albers executes a gray, black, and white Homage to the Square, a statement of neutrality: “someone else could have executed it.” Five hours; a list of what he does without: no smock, skylight, studio, palette, easel, brushes, medium, or canvas; an immaculate white linen suit while he works

One Sunday, wanting to work before his brushes and paints had arrived, Vicente cut up a color Sunday supplement and assembled a composition: his first collage, which supplied the motif for a later painting. A color Sunday supplement cut up and pasted Consequences: Since then he has never begun a collage as a project in itself, only as a diversion or an exercise for a painting; collages now make up half of his yearly output (about eight works in each medium)
1950 is the year Kline says his last word: his canvases suddenly change size to meet the scale of his concept. Consequences: Beginning of the large black-and-white canvases.

Still tied to representation in 1950, Kline draws figures, trains, horses, and landscapes in broad strokes of black paint alone; the line takes on such weight that the objective image is swamped by its own contours; he moves on to newspaper, then to 6-to-8-inch brushes, 6-to-8-foot canvases, and 5-gallon cans of paint; his first titles are those of the railroads of his childhood: Chief, Caboose. A 3-inch house-painting brush, then 6 to 8 inches; canvases of 6 to 8 feet; 5-gallon cans; black enamel; titles Chief, Caboose, Nijinsky, High Street Consequences: Elaine's formula: Rothko arrives at his style by gradual elimination, Kline by swallowing his past in one gulp

His sketches, now measured in feet, are drawn in black enamel on telephone-book pages and sheets of newspaper; he then works on several large canvases at once for days or months, repainting black into white and white into black to hollow out or build up the image. Telephone books, newspapers, black enamel

Commissioned by David Orr when Kline was already working in his new style; the radiant handling of the portrait gives him away. The dancer's head is tilted in a desperate, disjointed gesture, his blood-red eyes burning sadly in a face powdered a pasty white. Blood-red eyes, white-powdered face, tilted head Consequences: After which, purely bread-and-butter commissioned paintings in the 1950s, his black-and-whites being acclaimed but unsold

The American High Commissioner in Germany, based in Frankfurt, tells a Boston audience the story of a young girl who had come the week before to explain her plan for a school; he says he has no words to describe her voice and personality, and presents her case as a reason to have faith in the future of the German people. The visit took place at McCloy's house near Frankfurt. Consequences: McCloy becomes the project's champion.
Gruen goes over to the de Koonings' booth to tell Elaine how much he likes her writing Atmosphere: Smoke, beer, verbal liveliness Stakes: Recognition of Elaine as a writer, not just a painter's wife

Elaine tells him she wants to write about his color theories in an article; he replies that he will do a series based solely on color; two weeks later he has produced about a hundred paintings of the same format Words: “I will do this series, Homage to the Square, and it will just be based on color” Atmosphere: quiet determination, staggering productivity Stakes: the master becomes his student's subject

Turner demonstrates: he throws a piece, studies it slowly, puts it in the damp box, and puts it back on the wheel the next day to rework it. Richards learns to center clay and makes tumblers, slip trailing, sgraffito, and inlay. Words: Richards, inwardly: if she learned to throw “off the hump,” she would die of joy Atmosphere: wonder, desire, patience Stakes: the passage from one language (verbal) to another (manual) without her being aware of it

Hugs for Nick and Herb; the car goes down the road; Dawson feels a living identity leave his life; the school will have to adjust, one vital organ short. Atmosphere: joy at the departure for Princeton mixed with sadness Stakes: the first great departure; a premonition of his own

End-of-day drinks in Clem's office, assorted groups; Stamos sitting on the floor in the photograph; another snapshot (probably by Cora Ward): Clem and Helen with their heads under the waterfall of the natural pool. Atmosphere: gray “postwar days,” but a lively bohemian striving; scarce electricity, candles Stakes: the New York summer transplanted to the rustic South

Loud jazz; Mark comes in, ankles caught in colored streamers, tries to tear himself free, bursts into tears; the chorus urges him to come back and dance, pulls on a string; he frees himself, the music stops; in the silence he finds his night “alive”; he tells of Don Alter's Mondrian party, the strong punch, the tireless trumpet, the striped dancers visible through the walls; he recalls Anderson, Sally, Diana, those who were looking for him and whom he fled. Words: “Help me get these fucking strings off my legs”; “Turn off that noise! it's quiet— / Is it quiet?”; the chorus: “come back to the dance” Atmosphere: jazz punctuated by silences, streamers, festive claustrophobia, then a vibrant night Stakes: the individual against noisy sociability; desire hampered by too much choice

The hall is decorated with colored paper; Don Alter has built a set house after Mondrian; people dance while seeing the other dancers striped through the walls; the punch is strong, a trumpet plays without rest; the streamers tangle around their feet, and everyone falls out of rhythm, shrieking with joy; couples reshuffle and jealousies flare Words: The Chorus: “why are we standing out here in the cold?”; Mark: “more than one I wanted, and I touched”; the Chorus exclaims over the art that decorates an hour and dies in forgotten pleasure Atmosphere: gay, colorful, chaotic, primary colors around the narrator's shoulders when he closes his eyes Stakes: the community's happiness sours into crossed desires and hatreds (Jerry and Gwiffy Brown hate Mark)

Drawn by a cry in the woods, Mark finds an empty house with a fire burning and chairs set out for a meeting with no audience; the Dancer springs from the fire: a dead child who complains of being walled up in the house so that the community can exist; he tells of his escape one summer day (the herons flying up from the tree), dances his “new dance,” falls as if killed, then laughs and invites Mark; he kisses him gravely and vanishes; there is neither fire nor fireplace Words: Ghost: “Why have you locked me in this world, father?”; “the stones of the house are angry”; “Friend, isn't death in your heart too?”; Mark: “I wish to be dead, but do not choose to die”; Chorus: “Nay I am cheerful now. Let me die some other day.” Atmosphere: nocturnal, fantastic, terror, then ecstatic joy Stakes: Mark faces death at the heart of his disappointed love for the community and for Sally; he comes out of it loved and changed (“the Art is murder”)

The child shouts “Here comes the weapons carrier!” on seeing the army garbage truck arrive; his Quaker father slaps him; Oppenheimer, looking on, decides at that moment not to be a pacifist Words: The child: “Here comes the weapons carrier!” Atmosphere: The child's comic logic, the father's mute brutality, the young poet's irony Stakes: The culture clash between conventional Quakers and the avant-garde

Levi defends Goodman and suggests giving up the money-losing farm; Trayer, beside himself, hits Levi; a loud thud, and Levi gets up off the floor rubbing his jaw; Oppenheimer jumps on Trayer's back and stays there shouting insults; Johanna Jalowetz cheers from the sidelines; Goodman nicknames Oppenheimer “The Wild Bull of the Campus” Words: Oppenheimer: “You fucking bastard!”; Jalowetz: “You tell him!”; Levi later to Flola Shepard: he had not known that teaching was such a dangerous profession Atmosphere: Sudden violence, stupefaction, slapstick chaos Stakes: The physical breaking point between the old and the new Black Mountain

Several student meetings; a Navy veteran accuses Goodman of having urinated in public (he had peed behind a tree during softball); Oppenheimer retorts with the story of the old lady at the hotel and the clerk she invites to hang out of the window; the majority finally comes out for Goodman, but too slowly and too nastily Words: Oppenheimer, paraphrasing the old lady: climb up on the dresser and lean out, like me Atmosphere: Petty controversy, a half-comic witch trial Stakes: The slowness of the student vote gives the faculty a pretext for turning Goodman down

Just before Levi leaves, Huss offers to take him out to dinner and asks whom he wants to invite; Levi answers “Natasha,” the woman who led the campaign against him Words: Levi: “Natasha”; Dan Rice, later: “That's the philosopher in him” Atmosphere: The magnanimous melancholy of parting Stakes: Greatness of soul at the moment of defeat

Betty pleads passionately for Joe and Mary; Pete, believing he is voting like his wife, casts his ballot against Levi; back home, he is reproached for wanting to drive someone out out of personal dislike Words: Betty: no one should be driven out of Black Mountain out of personal distaste Atmosphere: Marital misunderstanding, retrospective anger Stakes: Principle against feeling within a couple

Merrill murmurs that it will be warmer in here; he undresses Rumaker, contemplates him under the harsh light, lays him on the mattress by the stove; undresses himself (plaid shirt, T-shirt, dungarees); a kiss like eating the juiciest peach; an abrupt sixty-nine that nearly makes him gag; then the first time from behind: Rumaker's homosexual experience ends in a simultaneous climax; lying there, Rumaker does not know whether he likes it; Merrill does not invite him to stay and offers to heat the water for a shower; Rumaker declines and walks down the road in the cold night Words: It will be warmer in here; the offer to turn on the water heater for a shower Atmosphere: Harsh light, an icy floor despite the stove, musky dampness, the dizziness of an unknown continent Stakes: The threshold: Rumaker crosses the door into sexuality and into an affair that will define his winter

After making love, under the quilt, they each tell their life stories until the windows grow light; Merrill reels off the list of his loves and then, longer, of his hatreds (Olson, Wes Huss, Wolpe); Rumaker listens docilely, ready to defend, inwardly disapproving but keeping quiet for fear of losing him Words: Olson an arrogant windbag who is destroying the school; Wolpe is to replace Lou Harrison, dismissed at Charles's instigation Atmosphere: The warm darkness of the quilt, trusting intimacy, the blinding pollen of love Stakes: Rumaker sacrifices his own judgments to love; the seeds of future conflicts

After a full day's work, the Alberses sit on the steps of their oxblood cottage and look at their peaceful Dörfchen of twin houses behind mowed lawns, theirs excepted Words: Josef to his friends: come visit our blood red Cape Cod cottage Atmosphere: Ordinary, almost ironic peace after sixteen years at Black Mountain Stakes: The transplanting of a couple of European artists into the America of housing developments

Albers takes Arnheim by the arm right on the platform and tells him that on arriving at Yale, his first statement was that there would be no more naked women, only squares. Words: “Listen, you know, when I came to Yale, the first thing I said was: 'No longer any naked women—only squares!'” Atmosphere: Complicity, humor, the friendship of two old Europeans. Stakes: Albers's self-definition: a break with the academic tradition of the nude.

Albers takes Arnheim by the arm right on the platform and tells him what he said on arriving at Yale. Words: “Listen, you know, when I came to Yale, the first thing I said was: 'No longer any naked women—only squares!'” Atmosphere: knowing good humor, an old man's banter

Albers has just resigned from Black Mountain College; Sawyer travels to New York to offer him the chairmanship of Yale's new Department of Design, while Gropius makes rival overtures for Harvard. Stakes: Albers's choice between Gropius's shadow at Harvard and a chairmanship still to be created at Yale.

Shortly after Rondal's suggestion, Cunningham turns up at the young couple's home with a jar of homemade Satsuma plum jam. Atmosphere: A warm, domestic gesture, with the garden as common ground. Stakes: The birth of the friendship that will transform the image of the artist-mother.

Still and Parsons select works at the house; in the months before the opening, Rauschenberg repaints the selected canvases dozens of times on an entirely different concept Words: He recalls being so naive and excited then, and Betty was surprised Atmosphere: The young artist's creative euphoria and recklessness Stakes: The conflict between the work sold and the work forever in progress

In the fall of 1950, they boldly walk in carrying as many canvases as they can; a religious series (Garden of Eden, Crucifixion and Reflection, Trinity); Parsons, at first stunned, is won over and offers a show Atmosphere: boldness and trepidation Stakes: first recognition from the art world

The couple decides to make a life-size image of Susan's little brother: discovering the blueprint process, photograms made with light, large-scale composition Words: “Bob and I thought big” Atmosphere: Inventive, close-knit Stakes: First use of life-size human figures in blueprint

Sitting outside, the former Moderator declares that a teacher arriving in the fall is gay; the others ask how he knows; he feigns shock, promises to prove it, and does. Words: he would pretend to be shocked, then say he would show us Atmosphere: the knowing curiosity of a spring afternoon Stakes: tipping the school into its homosexual period

Fall 1950: Olson, sick with uncertainty about how to proceed, reads manuscripts aloud before discussing them; he attributes a poem by Mark to Mary, and Mary sharply corrects him; forty years later the memory is still vivid and feelings still raw. Atmosphere: the initial clumsiness of the giant turned teacher Stakes: how a poet learns to teach, and what BMC forgives or does not

The day after the reading of Father, Dawson is in the kitchen when Mary, in a soft voice, pays him a compliment full of surprise and admiration and uses the word “writer.” Words: Paraphrased compliment: she calls him a writer. Atmosphere: Surprise and awe, an unforgettable soft voice; Dawson is twenty. Stakes: The founding recognition of his identity as a writer.

Dawson walks past an open door; the red-haired woman, her back to him, in half profile in a Vermeer light, a cigarette at her fingertips, is speaking in a low, persuasive voice to another woman out of sight inside; he knows who it is. Atmosphere: Vermeer light, a low persuasive voice, a closed night setting, mountain calm with an echo. Stakes: An image of desire and pursuit; a moment Dawson would like to film.

One sunny afternoon, Corny beckons to Dawson by the sink and shows him a six-inch thread with a wink; outside they laugh too hard to tie the thread around the wart; tying, sprinkling with dirt, eyes closed, the incantation three times; the hole dug, the thread laid in it as if it were hot and covered over; two weeks later they come back: the thread is gone; fits of laughter Words: Corny: it is a tough one, so they will give it time, say two weeks; then, that it is a bad wart Atmosphere: Uncontrollable laughter, complicity, spring Stakes: Motherly tenderness against Dawson's self-destruction

Frightened, Olson tells his dream in the morning: a street in broad daylight in Washington, a Soviet bomber in the sky, and he knows it is carrying the Bomb; he gazes at the lake, wide-eyed, asking what it means. Atmosphere: sacred anguish, “spellbound,” the lake in the morning Stakes: the Bomb enters the life of the college

In-the-round staging of a Cocteau play by M.C. Richards; June Rice Christensen plays the photographer, photographed by Hazel Larsen Archer from among the audience. Atmosphere: the intimacy of theater in the round, the audience as close as possible to the actors Stakes: the collapse of the boundary between stage and audience

De Kooning, suddenly worried about his Dutch accent, asks Motherwell to read his text to the group; the reading takes place twice. Words: The text: we do not put order into nature but into ourselves. Atmosphere: Embarrassment, friendship, a substitute voice. Stakes: The foreign artist and his language; friendship as a borrowed voice.

He paints standing, never sitting down, constantly moving back and forth between palette and easel, applying paint in broad, lightning gestures; the canvas is often finished in a few hours; if he is dissatisfied, he does not patch it but redoes the whole composition in a single movement. Words: “Making a picture is almost a physical struggle”; “A picture must be finished in one sweep”. Atmosphere: Nervous energy, speed, physical tension. Stakes: The painting as bodily struggle: the image of the painter in combat.

A long study of the motif before the first stroke; a small soft brush dipped in turpentine and then in blue and yellow to lay down the “architecture” of the motif in fine lines, like a blueprint; grounds rubbed in with gauze; a break with the initial drawing; a tic-tac-toe drawn so thin that the paint runs, the canvas tilted to steer the drips; pigments applied with the knife, with wrung-out gauze in dry-brush, glazes thinned with turpentine; a big stroke of deep blue crushed on with a brush held like a dagger; the paper backdrop collapses and shifts the objects; after three hours, fifteen brushes in his left hand; the next day, an eight-hour session, a red string of shapes on the left, the signature on the right. Words: “A picture must be finished in one sweep”; if he loses his ground, he has overshot his goal; painting, for him, is forming with color. Atmosphere: Feverish, physical, controlled; thick, wet paint in which the colors stay intact and separate. Stakes: The accident (the collapse of the backdrop) forcing the artist to obey nothing but the logic of the picture.

Arriving in February 1950, just turned twenty, already expelled from Cornell and the University of Chicago, he adopts Black Mountain at once but finds the Quaker presence very strange; seeing a Quaker slap his five-year-old child, who was shouting “Here comes the weapons carrier!” at the army garbage truck, he decides not to be a pacifist, just as he had decided at Cornell not to be a civil engineer Garbage truck: an army-surplus weapons carrier

Stoehr meets Goodman at the exact midpoint of his writing career; Goodman inscribes for him a copy of The Dead of Spring, self-published by Dave Dellinger's Libertarian Press. A book printed on the cheapest paper, with a plastic spiral binding and a yellow and black cardboard cover illustrated by his brother Percival, later scribbled on by Stoehr's young children, now in their fifties Consequences: In the year of his death, Goodman still considered The Dead of Spring his best work

First meeting: Goodman, forty years into a career that stretches from high school poems in 1927 to essays in 1972, inscribes for the young man a copy hot off Dave Dellinger's press; fifty years later, Stoehr still holds that yellowed, brittle volume Atmosphere: A modest, homemade object: the cheapest paper, a plastic spiral, a yellow and black cardboard cover Stakes: An overlooked masterpiece given to a stranger at a low point in a career

Gropius assures Albers that he is their first choice but warns that the administration wants a younger man at a lower salary; he even asks Albers's opinion of junior candidates competing with him. Albers answers with diplomatic contempt for all the suggestions. In June, Gropius informs him that for bureaucratic reasons he has not obtained the post. Letter of March 16, 1950: “You are tops in the field”. Consequences: Albers goes to Yale.

Faculty meetings of March 23 (student poll) and April 13 (faculty vote in favor of M.C. Richards and Fiore), then April, May, and June 1950, with board meetings on May 10 and June 1, 2, 7, and 8. Student poll; successive votes Consequences: The teaching staff is kept, then reshaped

Twenty-three artists selected by Greenberg and Schapiro for this show of the rising generation; Weldon Kees notes in The Nation that the dominant 57th Street galleries ignored them and praises the enormous spirit, optimism, and love of painting of the whole. 23 artists selected Consequences: high point of Elaine's year

York, Albers's immediate predecessor as head of the painting department, resigns in protest on learning of the impending changes, which he considers intolerably stupid, narrow, and intellectually dishonest. Consequences: The way is clear for Sawyer to offer Albers the chair officially, by letter in June 1950

Open letter dated May 20, 1950, to Roland L. Redmond, president of the Met, signed by eighteen painters (including de Kooning) and ten sculptors, protesting the museum's lack of commitment to advanced art: for roughly a hundred years, only advanced art has made any consequential contribution to civilization. 18 painters and 10 sculptors signed. Consequences: Life magazine runs a story; the photograph of the “Irascibles” on January 15, 1951.

The Board of Fellows (eight of the twenty-two faculty members, dominated by conservatives) votes by secret ballot not to rehire the Levis and Joe Fiore. Fiore is accused of setting a bad example: in love with the student Mary Fitton, he lives with her although he is married, his wife being confined in an asylum near Asheville; his critics fear above all a suicide and bad publicity. The vote against M.C. is in fact a vote against Levi: she is identified with her husband. 8 of the 22 faculty members; secret ballot; asylum near Asheville Consequences: Indignation among most of the faculty; Joe and Mary will later marry
Nick Cernovich, Student Moderator, organizes a student poll: a large majority favors rehiring M.C., but also Levi and Fiore. Consequences: Contradicts the Board's purge

The faculty works out a compromise: a rector guaranteed three years, sharing with the Board the powers of appointment and rehiring, responsible with the treasurer for the annual budget (subject to the Board's approval), not teaching and devoted to administration. Three-year term Consequences: Makes possible the offers to Ballou and Huss

At the end of June, the faculty offers the post of rector to Richard Ballou, director of education of the Ethical Culture schools, and the post of business manager (and drama teacher) to Wesley Huss, a Quaker friend of Don Warrington's who had worked with the Friends Service Committee and the Hedgerow Theater.

After their trip to New Orleans, Tom and Michael hitchhike back to the college, arriving late on a Sunday afternoon, starving and exhausted. There was nothing left to eat in their kitchen at Meadows Inn except a box of Quaker Oats, which Tom cooked on a Coleman stove. Consequences: Reunion with Charles Olson, who welcomes them with relief.

A young blond driver with a choirboy's face picks them up, invites them to eat a hamburger, claims to check a tire, and disappears with their suitcases while they are ordering. Tom had offered to pay for the burger, coffee, and a slice of pie. The thief's hamburger left cold on the counter. Consequences: Rumaker loses a week's worth of clothes, his razor, his toothbrush, and the only new thing he owned: a suitcase given to him by his mother. He comes home with less than nothing.

Charles comes past Meadows Inn, climbing carefully over the pine roots on the path, and talks to Tom and Michael through the window screen to welcome them, insisting on how glad he is to see them again. He seemed to have been watching for their return. Tom tells about the trip and the theft; Charles, who loves a good story, listens eagerly. Consequences: Rumaker feels an overwhelming sense of safety on returning to Black Mountain ground.

With his GI pay, Tom buys a gray 1950 Buick in good condition, with three decorative chrome “portholes” on each side of the hood. The chrome “portholes” are what sold the model to Tom (and to millions of others). Car parked on the grass in front of Meadows Inn. Consequences: Makes possible errands in town, beer outings to Ma Peak's, and movies in Asheville.

After the trip, Tom buys a gray 1950 Buick with his GI discharge pay, drawn by the three small decorative chrome portholes on each side of the hood. Car parked on the grass in front of Meadows Inn. Makes possible ice runs, groceries in town, beer at Ma Peak's, movies in Asheville. Consequences: Tom takes off in his new toy at every opportunity.

A few days after returning from New Orleans, Rumaker discovers he has caught crabs, a souvenir of his Cajun. He will end up laughing at the episode as part of his education, like the whole trip, “on and off campus.”

Richards translates Cocteau's Knights of the Round Table (1937), translates and directs his surrealist comedy Marriage on the Eiffel Tower (1923) in June, and directs Yeats's The Death of Cuchulain the same month. Printed program of The Death of Cuchulain dated June 4, 1950

The Board votes by secret ballot not to rehire M.C.; the faculty is stunned and M.C. thunderstruck; she raises a terrible storm Words: “an absolute thunderbolt”; her love of the place was so unquestioned that she could not imagine being dismissed Atmosphere: shock, indignation Stakes: a political purge disguised as an administrative measure

They climb the outside stairs like cat burglars; the Cajun protects his new lime-green sheets with a blanket; he spends a long time in the bathroom (an enema); he comes back naked, tanned all over, and lies on his stomach; after the act, he goes out again to rinse off; he finds a spot of K-Y on a sheet and scrubs it with a soapy sponge, clicking his tongue; he tries to come but fails; he admits his block with self-mockery. Words: “They're new and I don' want 'em to git stained”. “Ahm all greased and ready, baby”. “Maybe Ahm just an assman like Miz Peppah and not a cocksman”. Atmosphere: Moonlight through the shutters, the scent of tropical flowers, slow ceiling fans, feline nervousness, tenderness mixed with anxiety. Stakes: The Cajun's sexual humiliation, the constant fear of the 1950s, the loneliness of two men in a sensual and dangerous city.

On the morning of departure (Saturday), the Cajun takes Michael to the garish drugstore where he works; chicory coffee for Michael, a Coke for himself; he introduces Michael to his coworkers, who look at them with irony. Words: The Cajun, with a touch of defiance: “Yeah, Ah slept with 'im”. Atmosphere: Unromantic fluorescent light, nervousness in the Cajun's eyes, that old 1950s fear, even in New Orleans. Stakes: The gap between the night of desire and the day of social fear.

The young blond driver with a choirboy's face offers them a burger in a small back-street café; he claims to check a tire; they order three hamburgers; they use the restroom; the driver's burger grows cold; Tom goes out to check and comes back aghast: the man and their suitcases are gone; they wait in vain. Words: “Ahm so famished ma' belly's kissin' ma' backbone”. “That's mighty white a' ya”. “Maybe he'll be back”, Tom says weakly. Atmosphere: A dark back street, a creaking screen door, the slow realization of the deception, shame. Stakes: The loss of their belongings, a blow to Rumaker's pride, a crack in the two friends' closeness.

Late Sunday afternoon, starving, they find only Quaker Oats, which Tom cooks on the Coleman; Charles comes by, skipping over the pine roots, and talks to them through the window screen, glad to see them again; Tom tells about the trip and the theft, and Charles listens eagerly. Words: Charles insists on how glad he is to see them again. Atmosphere: The warmth of homecoming, safety regained, Rumaker's shame at the thought of Charles knowing they had been duped. Stakes: The contrast between the deceptive outside world and the refuge of the college.

In mid-July, Ballou turns down the rectorship, citing the confusion between community and education at Black Mountain and the faculty's indecision about the rector's role beyond raising funds. Wes Huss, on the other hand, accepts the post of business manager. Consequences: The conservatives give up all hope of a responsible reorganization

During the long, lazy summer afternoons, Tom and Michael swim in the Snake River whirlpool and sunbathe on the rocks. Hostile farmers' sons sometimes throw stones at them from the bushes. The water teems with creatures that Tom calls “newts” to reassure Michael, but that look like snakes. Consequences: The sun turns them as dark as the earth.

After lunch, a large filling falls out and the tooth starts to hurt horribly. Rumaker panics and knocks at Charles's back door; he is the only one with a car at the time. Charles is lying on his bed (dressed, this time), perhaps after his own breakfast. He is annoyed, finding it a nuisance, an imposition. Rumaker has to beg twice. Consequences: Charles reluctantly agrees to take him in his old Ford convertible, silent and sullen during the drive.

On the way, they pass Black laundresses sweating behind a rusty screen door. The dentist, a small bald man in a white coat, is direct and efficient. An upstairs office in a brick building, a narrow staircase. Cost: a few dollars. Charles stays silent on the way back. Consequences: The pain stops. Rumaker is grateful despite Charles's silence.

An ordinary dark-haired playwright of about thirty, passing through, reads a pacifist play at a Sunday evening program. Charles begins to snicker, softly at first, then loudly enough for the author to hear, and the audience follows. The playwright, sure of himself at first, casts alarmed glances, reads at top speed, then slips away into the night. Wes Huss, the only real pacifist on board, stays silent, his face controlled. Consequences: The playwright was never seen again. Charles restates his rejection of pacifism in the next class.

Broke after the trip and the theft, Rumaker confides his worries to Charles. Charles insists: he must tighten his belt even further, and suggests applying at the Swannanoa blanket mills, rumored to be hiring for the night shift. A bus supposedly runs on the county road near the VA hospital. Michael doubts it runs at night. Fear of missing Olson's morning class (“Reading the Newspaper”). Consequences: Rumaker inwardly refuses (past factory experience, the shipyard with his father). Charles, sensing his refusal, then offers him $5 to wash his windows and dust his books.

Charles comes back furious from an errand in town with two-year-old Kate, because a shopkeeper was too harsh with the child, who was rummaging in the candy or something else. Kate did not understand the woman's anger. Consequences: Charles lets the whole community know of his anger.

A pacifist playwright passing through (dark-haired, ordinary, early thirties) reads one of his plays at a Sunday evening program in the basement of the Studies Building. Charles snickers, softly at first, then louder and louder, and the audience follows. The author, sure of himself at first, speeds up his reading and slips away into the night, never to be seen again. Wes Huss, the only real pacifist on board, stays silent, his face controlled. Rumaker joins the laughers, having become, in his own words, a regular Black Mountain thug. Consequences: In class, Charles restates his rejection of pacifism and raises again the question of the marauders on the hill and the marauders within.

Broke after New Orleans and the theft, Rumaker confides his money worries to Charles, who again recommends applying at the Swannanoa blanket mills (rumored to be hiring for the night shift), so that he can attend his daytime classes, including “Reading the Newspaper.” A bus supposedly runs on the county road near the VA hospital, but Rumaker doubts it runs at night. An 8-to-10-hour night shift. Rumaker has already done factory jobs (including the shipyard with his father) and inwardly refuses. Consequences: Charles, seeing his refusal, offers him $5 to wash his windows and dust the books in the living room bookcase.

Rumaker, panicked by a lost filling, knocks at the screen door; Charles is lying on his bed, dressed, annoyed; Rumaker has to beg twice; Charles reluctantly agrees; a silent drive in the Ford convertible; a visit to a direct and efficient dentist; a silent return. Atmosphere: Throbbing pain, shyness broken by urgency, Charles's sullen silence, Rumaker's shame. Stakes: The poor student's dependence on the rectorship, the imbalance of power, conditional generosity.

Sunday evening; the playwright begins his reading with confidence; Charles snickers softly, then louder, and the audience follows; Rumaker joins the laughers; the author rushes his reading, casts panicked glances over his pages, gallops to the end, and vanishes into the night. Atmosphere: Pack laughter, the reader's panic, Wes Huss frozen and silent. Stakes: The college's social cruelty, Olson's power over the group, Rumaker's complicit cowardice.

After Rumaker's polite refusal of the mills, Charles, as if it had just occurred to him (though he had probably read the refusal in his face), offers $5 to wash his windows and dust the books in the living room. Words: Rumaker thinks that five dollars, a small fortune, would let him eat for a few more weeks. Atmosphere: Embarrassment, gratitude, fragile dignity. Stakes: Charity disguised as work, the last-minute rescue of a student on the verge of leaving.

With Olson and Connie away on a visit, Dawson and LaFarge occupy the little brick house for two days, sleep in sleeping bags in the hall, explore the library, take showers in the basement, and eat what they bought at the neighborhood market. Sleeping bag or blankets in the hall; a shower without a curtain in the basement, cement floor; dishes done in a tiny sink Consequences: On his return, Olson wakes them and tells them they must leave; Dawson stays in D.C. with Ken and Neil Noland.

When the couple returns unexpectedly, Olson comes in while the two young men are still asleep on the hall floor; Dawson wakes and sits up, sees the bathroom door open; Olson, naked, hairy, immense, plants himself on the landing three steps up, the kitchen at an angle behind him, tells them they must leave, grinning, eyes shining at their astonishment, then disappears into the next room; they fold the sheets and blankets and pack their bags. Words: He tells them they have to leave: “okay, get out”. Atmosphere: Dawn, amused embarrassment, the blushes and laughter of the two young men Stakes: Olson's physical, childlike authority over his former students

The two go down the narrow staircase hidden behind a tiny door, doubled over with laughter at the thought of the giant Olson on those steps; each takes a shower without a curtain, on the cement, telling himself that not showering in Olson's shower would have been unthinkable; they clearly had to stoop and twist, just as he did. Atmosphere: Shared giggles, the stolen intimacy of the master's house
Josef is invited to chair the Department of Design at Yale University; the Alberses leave BMC for Connecticut. Consequences: End of their BMC period

After Sawyer and Howe's offer in New York in the spring of 1950, Albers begins in September 1950 and settles with Anni on the outskirts of New Haven. Letter from Osborn to Albers (April 1950) pressing him with Sawyer; William Huff reports that Kahn, when consulted, was sold on Albers and enchanted by Anni, “straight from the Old Testament”; Switzer had proposed a department of Basic Design and Sculpture under Albers. Consequences: Beginning of the Yale period (1950-1958).

Alvin Eisenman, also typographer of Yale University Press, launches the program in the fall of 1950, with an undergraduate component added at Albers's insistence. Renamed “Graphic Design” in 1959, it puts Yale in the front rank of the field; its graduates spread Albers's ideas throughout the country. Eisenman describes Albers as “very interested in the program, very, very helpful, and kindly”
The two programs become degree programs in September 1950.

Twombly meets Rauschenberg at the Art Students League in New York in the fall of 1950; they quickly become friends, and Twombly follows Rauschenberg to Black Mountain the next summer. Consequences: Twombly arrives at BMC, summer 1951
De Kooning commutes to New Haven to teach at Yale during the fall of 1950. A weekly commute between New York and New Haven.

Thanksgiving dinner 1950 takes place on a stage set representing the first-level terrace of the Eiffel Tower. After the meal, the community attends Jean Cocteau's play-ballet Les Mariés de la tour Eiffel (1921), translated by M.C. Richards. The absurd plot: a photographer tries to photograph a wedding party; an ostrich seizes his camera and runs off; a hunter with a rifle chases the bird through the latticework of the tower; a lion devours a guest, a cyclist asks the way to Chatou, a bather from Trouville appears; telegrams fall from the sky (one shot down in midflight); a General tells of a hunting expedition in Africa with a pie covered in wasps; finally the bride and groom and their guests vanish into the camera, swallowed whole, and the camera leaves the stage trailing its bellows like a wagon. Set: the first-level terrace of the Eiffel Tower; a giant camera on stage, large enough to hold the wedding party under its pleated skirt; June Rice Christensen in a checked jacket and a voluminous wig, on a ladder behind the shutter; through the openings in the bellows one sees the guests waving handkerchiefs and, below, feet walking; the camera leaves the stage trailing its bellows like a wagon. Consequences: Hazel Larsen Archer photographs the performance, the image that opens the study: a camera photographing a camera.
